The text then shifts to glial cells, correcting historical ratio estimates to modern findings of roughly 1:1 ratios in some regions while noting regional variation. It identifies four major CNS glial types: astrocytes (regulating ions, nutrients, connections), microglia (immune defense and phagocytosis), ependymal cells (producing cerebrospinal fluid), and oligodendrocytes (forming myelin sheaths to enhance neuronal function).
topics: Soma function: housing nucleus, cytoplasm, and protein machinery
Dendrite structure: branched extensions receiving signals at synapses
Axon characteristics: extending from soma, carrying electrical signals, variable lengths
Axon terminal role: releasing neurotransmitters across synapses
Four major glial types in the central nervous system
Brain astrocyte networks: ion concentration regulation, nutrient supply, connection control
Microglia: immune function, phagocytosis against infection/cellular damage, regulation of new connections
concepts: some human and other primate brain regions

source_context.text: Four major glial types occur in the central nervous system. Brain astrocyte networks regulate ion concentrations around neurons, supply nutrients, and help control new neuronal connections. Microglia, the brain's principal immune cells, mainly act as phagocytes against infection and cellular damage and also regulate new connections.
